body.stem: You run the webSS scale set in resource group app-rg, and a seasonal traffic peak requires the fleet to grow to about 900 instances. Every attempt to scale out is refused by the platform well before that point, and the business deadline is close. Which change should you make?

exhibit.text:
Scale set name        : webSS
Resource group        : app-rg
Region                : East US 2
Orchestration mode    : Flexible
Image                 : Managed image
Current instance count: 250
Required instance count: 900
Autoscale rules       : 3, host-based on Percentage CPU

options.text: Update the scale set's image to a marketplace image or a custom image stored in the Azure Compute Gallery, which supports 1,000 instances
Enable automatic instance repairs, which replaces an unhealthy instance with the same image or a golden copy, so the fleet scales up on its own
Spread the scale set across availability zones in Azure so a datacenter failure does not stop the workload
Add a virtual machine scaling profile to the scale set so autoscale can use the current image to create the additional instances

explanation.correct: Scale sets that run from a managed image are capped at 600 instances, which is why scale-out on webSS is refused before the fleet can reach 900. Marketplace images and custom images stored in the Azure Compute Gallery support up to 1,000 instances, so moving the scale set off the managed image onto one of those sources lifts the ceiling above the 900 instances the peak requires.

perChoice.b: Automatic instance repairs deal with unhealthy instances; they do not change the image-based ceiling on how many instances a scale set may run. Turning them on leaves the scale set exactly as limited as before, so the scale-out request would still be refused.
perChoice.c: Availability Zones distribute the instances of a scale set across datacenters for failure protection. They have no bearing on the maximum instance count, which is determined by the kind of image the fleet runs from, so the scale-out refusals continue.
perChoice.d: A virtual machine scaling profile tells autoscale what configuration the added instances should have, and it must exist for autoscaling to work at all. It does not change the ceiling on total instance count, so defining one would not stop the platform from rejecting the scale-out.

body.stem: You have the scale set shown in the exhibit running in resource group prod-rg. You need it to run a workload that combines Spot with on-demand capacity, and you also need to host an application that today runs as an Availability Set. Which change should you make?

options.text: Change the orchestration mode of the existing scale set to flexible with a portal update, then add the Availability Set application to it.
Enable Spot capacity for the existing scale set with a portal update, and keep the Availability Set application running where it is today.
Add a second scale set in the same resource group with uniform orchestration, and place the on-demand capacity there.
Build a replacement scale set with flexible orchestration, then bring the Availability Set application and the Spot and on-demand capacity into it.

explanation.correct: The orchestration mode is chosen when a scale set is created and can never be changed or updated afterwards, so the Uniform scale set shown in the exhibit cannot be converted in place. Flexible orchestration is the mode suited to deployments that combine Spot and on-demand VMs and to lifting an application that currently runs as an Availability Set into the fleet, so the only way to satisfy both requirements is to build a new scale set with flexible orchestration and move the Availability Set application across.

perChoice.a: No portal update can switch an existing scale set from Uniform to Flexible orchestration; the mode is fixed at creation time, so this change cannot be applied to the fleet in the exhibit.
perChoice.b: Enabling Spot allocation does not alter the orchestration mode of the scale set, and leaving the Availability Set application outside the fleet fails the requirement to host it in the scale set.
perChoice.c: A second scale set that also runs in Uniform orchestration keeps the same limitations that block the required deployment model, and it still leaves the Availability Set application unhosted.

body.stem: You are deploying the scale set described below into resource group app-rg. The portal stops the deployment with a validation failure, so no resources are created. You need the scale set deployed with the same name, region, orchestration, image and starting instance count. Which change should you make?

rows: Failed validation (InvalidParameterValue): the administrator credential was rejected.

options.text: Set the administrator password to at least 12 characters using at least three of the four character classes (lowercase, uppercase, digits, and special characters).
Set the administrator password to at least 12 characters using only lowercase letters and digits.
Keep the administrator password as entered and switch the administrator account to an SSH public key.
Set the administrator password to at least 8 characters using all four of the character classes.

explanation.correct: The administrator credential for a scale set must be a password of at least 12 characters that satisfies three of the four complexity rules (one lowercase letter, one uppercase letter, one digit and one special character). The value shown in the exhibit, 'summer2026', is only 10 characters and uses just two of the four classes, so validation rejects it. The correct option satisfies both the length and the complexity requirement, so the deployment can proceed with every other field unchanged.

perChoice.b: Length alone is not enough: this value draws on two of the four character classes, and the password must satisfy three of the four, so validation still fails.
perChoice.c: An SSH public key is an alternative credential for a Linux OS disk image. This scale set uses a Windows image, so the administrator credential must be a password that meets the length and complexity rules, and the rejected value cannot simply be retained.
perChoice.d: Covering all four character classes does not compensate for falling below the minimum length: the password must be at least 12 characters, so an 8-character value is still rejected.

body.stem: You have the scale set and the autoscale rule shown in the exhibit running in resource group app-rg. The rule only reacts to platform counters, so the fleet grows even while end users are struggling, and it stays flat while they are struggling badly. You need the fleet to grow automatically when users experience slow page loads, long response times, or abnormal session counts, and the operations team will not accept a solution that relies on counters collected inside the guest with a storage account behind them. Which metric source should you configure for the rule?

options.text: Application Insights metrics
Azure diagnostics extension metrics
Host-based metrics from the scale set
Azure Service Bus queue metrics

explanation.correct: The rule needs a source that reports what end users experience. Application Insights is the documented source for end-user signals such as response time, page load performance and session counts, so pointing the rule's metric source at Application Insights makes the fleet grow on slow page loads and long response times instead of on platform counters alone. The Azure diagnostics extension (in-guest counters plus a storage account) and Service Bus queue sources are ruled out by the stated constraints, and host-based metrics carry no end-user signal at all.

perChoice.b: The Azure diagnostics extension is an agent that runs inside the VM and publishes in-guest performance counters, for example AverageReadTime for disks and PercentIdleTime for CPU, to storage. It requires a storage account and configured performance counters, which the operations team has excluded, and it still exposes no page-load or response-time data.
perChoice.c: Host-based metrics describe how the instances are performing at the platform level (Percentage CPU, Network In, Network Out, disk read/write counters, CPU credit counters) and need no agents, but they say nothing about page loads or response times, so the fleet would still ignore end-user experience.
perChoice.d: A Service Bus queue source scales on the number of messages the web tier posts to a queue, so it only works if that tier publishes such messages. Nothing is being posted to a queue here, and queue length would not reflect slow page loads or long response times.

body.stem: You have the scale set and the autoscale profile shown in the exhibit running in resource group app-rg. Operations has funded a fixed size for Saturday's promotion, and the fleet must be at that size whenever the rule fires, even if someone has manually resized the fleet earlier in the morning. Which scale-out action should you configure for the rule?

rows: Baseline capacity the team wants afterwards

options.text: Increase count by 18
Increase percent by 150
Increase count to 30
Decrease count to 30

explanation.correct: The keyed action is the target-count scale-out operation: it creates as many instances as required to reach the desired number, so the fleet lands on the 30 instances funded for the promotion every time the rule fires, no matter what the capacity was beforehand.

perChoice.a: This action adds a fixed batch of VMs on every firing, so it only happens to reach 30 when the fleet is at exactly 12 beforehand; after a manual resize the fleet would still miss the funded event size.
perChoice.b: This action grows the fleet proportionally to whatever capacity it currently has, so the result changes with the starting size and the funded 30-instance event size is not guaranteed.
perChoice.d: This is a scale-in operation: it removes instances down to a minimum number and cannot be used to add capacity when the rule fires.

body.stem: You have the scale set and its autoscale profile shown in the exhibit running in resource group prod-rg. Every Monday at 09:00 the workload becomes far heavier for roughly half an hour, and during the first 10 to 15 minutes of that heavy period users report slow responses, because the fleet only starts adding instances once the CPU counter has stayed above its threshold for a while. You know this demand pattern in advance and need the extra compute already running when it begins, and removed again once the load drops. Which change should you make?

rows: Average Percentage CPU greater than 75 for 10 minutes

options.text: Lower the metric threshold on the existing autoscale rule so it reacts sooner.
Add a second autoscale rule based on the Network In metric that adds instances when traffic rises.
Change the scaling mode to Manual and set the instance count to 12.
Add a schedule-based autoscale rule that pre-provisions instances ahead of time.

explanation.correct: Because the heavy load is known in advance, the capacity has to exist before the load arrives rather than after it is measured. A schedule-based autoscale rule adds the instances at a defined point in the week, so the extra compute is already running when the demand increases, and it can scale back in when the load drops. The single metric rule in the exhibit cannot do this: it reacts only after the CPU metric stays above the threshold for the configured period, which is exactly the delay users are seeing at the start of the busy hour.

perChoice.a: Lowering the threshold makes the existing rule fire earlier, but the fleet still reacts only after the CPU metric has remained above the threshold for the configured period, so the same delay at the start of the heavy period remains. It also makes the rule scale in more eagerly when load falls.
perChoice.b: A second metric-based rule is still reactive: instances are added only after traffic crosses the threshold and stays there for the configured period, so capacity is not ready when the load first increases and the early slowdown is unchanged.
perChoice.c: A fixed instance count runs the larger fleet continuously, wasting capacity and cost in quiet periods, and it prevents any rule from reacting when demand changes. It also gives no automatic way to shrink the fleet after the heavy period ends.

body.stem: You have the scale set shown in the exhibit running in resource group app-rg. Browsers cannot open the site over HTTPS because the instances serve plain HTTP and carry no certificate, and every request is handed to whichever instance happens to answer, so /api and /media traffic is mixed together. You need a single entry point that decrypts the HTTPS traffic before it reaches the instances and that directs each URL path to the right group of instances. Which change should you make?

rows: Azure load balancer, TCP pass-through on port 443
HTTP on port 80 only, no certificate installed on any instance
2 groups: group A for /api, group B for /media

options.text: Front the scale set with Azure Application Gateway, so it decrypts the HTTPS traffic and routes each URL path to the correct instance group.
Front the scale set with Azure load balancer, so it decrypts the HTTPS traffic and routes each URL path to the correct instance group.
Front the scale set with Azure Application Gateway, so it only passes connections through to the instances and leaves the HTTPS and URL path handling to them.
Front the scale set with Azure load balancer, so it only passes connections through to the instances and leaves the HTTPS and URL path handling to them.

explanation.correct: Azure Application Gateway is the component that can sit in front of a scale set and perform advanced layer-7 handling plus TLS termination: it decrypts the incoming HTTPS request before it reaches the instances, so the instances need no certificate, and it can send each URL path to a different backend pool, which matches the two instance groups (group A for /api, group B for /media). The Azure load balancer used today only offers basic layer-4 traffic distribution, so it cannot do either of those jobs.

perChoice.b: The Azure load balancer performs basic layer-4 traffic distribution only. It can forward connections to the instances, but it cannot decrypt the encrypted request on their behalf and it cannot inspect the URL path, so browsers would still fail on the HTTPS request and the two instance groups would keep receiving mixed traffic.
perChoice.c: Application Gateway is the right product, but this configuration only passes connections through and leaves the HTTPS and URL path handling to the instances. In this scale set the instances run plain HTTP with no certificate installed, so they cannot accept the encrypted request or split traffic by URL path on their own.
perChoice.d: This pairs the product that only offers basic layer-4 distribution with pass-through behaviour, so nothing in the request path decrypts the HTTPS traffic or separates the /api and /media requests.

body.stem: You have the scale set shown in the exhibit running in resource group app-rg. Every instance currently runs in one zone of the westeurope region, so when that zone goes down the whole service stops answering requests. You need the workload to keep serving traffic when one zone fails. Which change should you make?

exhibit.text:
Scale set app-vmss  (resource group app-rg)

  Region                      : westeurope
  Orchestration               : Flexible
  Instance distribution       : all instances in one zone of the region
  Platform fault domain count : 3
  Instance count              : 6
  Load balancing              : Azure load balancer (backend pool app-vmss)

options.text: Turn on zone placement for the scale set so the instances are spread across the Availability Zones of the region and the fleet survives the loss of one zone.
Raise the platform fault domain count from 3 to 5 so the instances are spread over more fault domains inside the region.
Move the scale set to a different Availability Zone and keep every instance running in that one zone.
Add the instances to an Availability Set so the platform spreads them over separate fault domains inside the region.

explanation.correct: A scale set by itself does not protect against the loss of a data center; spreading the instances over the Availability Zones of the region (zone placement) is what does. With instances distributed over several zones, the failure of one zone's facility still leaves instances in the other zones to serve traffic. Fault domains and Availability Sets only isolate VMs from each other inside a region, so they cover host and rack failures but not the loss of a zone's data center.

perChoice.b: Fault domains isolate VMs from one another inside a region, which covers host, rack and similar platform failures. Adding more fault domains to spread across improves that isolation, but every instance still sits in one zone, so a zone-level data-center failure takes the whole fleet down.
perChoice.c: Relocating the scale set to another Availability Zone and keeping every instance there only moves the single point of failure to a different zone; the service still stops completely when that one zone fails.
perChoice.d: An Availability Set spreads VMs across fault domains within a region rather than across Availability Zones, and the instances of a scale set are not members of an Availability Set, so this change would not survive the loss of a zone's data center either.

body.stem: You have the scale set api-vmss running in resource group app-rg, and four new autoscale rules are planned for it. You need every rule to react to the data described below, and each rule carries its own constraint. Match each rule to the source that can supply its trigger data.

rows: The platform's own reading of processor utilization rises above 80%
No software may be installed inside the instances
Disk read time observed inside the guest exceeds 40 ms
The readings must be stored in a storage account
Users report slow page loads and unusual session counts
The signal must come from instrumentation embedded in the code
The workload publishes more than 500 pending work messages
The trigger must read those messages directly

slots.label: Rule 1: processor utilization trigger
Rule 2: in-guest disk read time trigger
Rule 3: end-user experience trigger
Rule 4: workload message trigger

explanation.correct: Rule 1 takes its processor reading from the platform itself, which is what host-based metrics provide for the current scale set: they show how the instances are performing on CPU, memory, or disk access without installing or configuring any agent or extra data collection in the guest, which matches the 'no software inside the instances' constraint. Rule 2 needs detailed in-guest counters such as disk read time, which come from the Azure diagnostics extension: an agent that runs inside the VM, monitors performance, writes those counters (for example AverageReadTime for disks and PercentIdleTime for CPU) to Azure storage, and therefore requires a storage account plus configured performance counters. Rule 3 depends on what end users actually experience, so Application Insights applies: an instrumentation package in the application streams telemetry such as response times, page load performance, and session counts. Rule 4 is driven by the workload's own messages, so an Azure Service Bus queue is the source, because the application or other components can post messages on a queue that are then consumed to trigger autoscale rules.

perChoice.i1: Fits Rule 4. An Azure Service Bus queue is a source the application or other components can post messages to, and those messages are then read to trigger autoscale rules, which matches a trigger based on the workload's own pending work messages.
perChoice.i2: Fits Rule 1. Host-based metrics come from the current scale set and need no agents or extra data collection configured in the instances, so rules can react to processor utilization, memory demand, or disk access while nothing is installed in the guest.
perChoice.i3: Fits Rule 3. Application Insights is an instrumentation package installed in the application that streams telemetry to Azure, covering response times, page load performance, and session counts, which is what the end-user experience rule needs.
perChoice.i4: Fits Rule 2. The Azure diagnostics extension is an agent that runs inside the virtual machine, saves performance counters such as AverageReadTime for disks and PercentIdleTime for CPU to Azure storage, and needs storage accounts and configured performance counters, so it satisfies the in-guest disk read time requirement with storage behind it.

body.stem: You administer the scale sets listed in the exhibit for the platform team, and you are rewriting their autoscale profiles so that every rule performs one specific change in the number of running instances. Match each requirement below with the scale action that implements it.

slots.label: api-vmss must add a fixed number of extra instances whenever demand outruns capacity
batch-vmss must add a share of its present size whenever demand outruns capacity, so the reaction stays noticeable
When the Saturday promotion starts, api-vmss must run exactly the size operations funded, regardless of the size it had beforehand
api-vmss must remove a fixed number of instances whenever demand falls away
batch-vmss must remove a share of its present size whenever demand falls away, so the saving stays worthwhile
During quiet periods, api-vmss must run exactly the size agreed with operations as the floor

explanation.correct: The fixed-number actions suit api-vmss, which never exceeds 20 instances, because a small change to such a fleet is clearly visible; the share-based actions suit batch-vmss, which runs in the hundreds, because a fixed change there would barely shift performance or cost. The two 'exactly the size' requirements ask for the fleet to land on a specific number (the funded maximum for the promotion, the agreed floor in quiet periods) no matter what its size was beforehand, and only the 'count to' actions guarantee that outcome.

perChoice.i1: Matches the api-vmss requirement to add a fixed number of extra instances: that fleet is small (5 running, 20 maximum), so a fixed change has a visible effect on performance and cost.
perChoice.i2: Matches the batch-vmss requirement to add a share of the current size: that fleet is large (800 running, 1000 maximum), where a fixed change would barely move performance or cost.
perChoice.i3: Matches the promotion requirement for api-vmss: the fleet ends at exactly the funded size whatever its size was beforehand, which is what a 'count to' action guarantees.
perChoice.i4: Matches the api-vmss requirement to remove a fixed number of instances when demand falls: on a small fleet a fixed reduction is a meaningful, visible change.
perChoice.i5: Matches the batch-vmss requirement to remove a share of the current size when demand falls: on a large fleet the saving must scale with the fleet, because a fixed reduction would be negligible.
perChoice.i6: Matches the quiet-period requirement for api-vmss: the fleet is brought to exactly the agreed floor rather than losing an arbitrary number of instances.

body.stem: You administer the scale sets in the exhibit for the platform team. Every owning team has raised a requirement, and the list of items below contains the change or the fact that answers it. Match every requirement to the item that satisfies it.

rows: Autoscale conditions are saved and enabled; the fleet size has not changed once since creation
26 trigger conditions are listed for one scale set, and the portal refuses to save the changes
Flexible orchestration; a quorum-based database that lost quorum during a platform maintenance event
Nobody has written down when this workload gets busy
Production workload; the fleet is being re-provisioned using new persistent storage
Finance is reviewing what the platform puts on the monthly bill for the fleet

items.text: Add a virtual machine scaling profile that defines the configuration of the instances to add
Limit the autoscale rules of a single scale set to 20 or fewer
Distribute the instances across fault domains within the region
Spread the instances across Availability Zones inside the scale set
Predictive AI autoscale adjusts the instance count automatically from usage patterns it discovers
Back the scale set's data volumes with Azure managed disks
The scale set itself carries no extra charge; you pay only for the resources it consumes

slots.label: checkout-vmss — the fleet must grow and shrink by itself
media-vmss — the listed conditions must fit what the platform accepts for one scale set
ledger-vmss — the fleet must not lose quorum during one maintenance event and must stay in its current location
batch-vmss — the fleet must resize itself around a demand rhythm that nobody on the team has identified
prod-vmss — the fleet must use the option that the platform points to for production workloads
finance-vmss — the finance team needs to know what the platform puts on the monthly bill for the fleet

explanation.correct: Each requirement maps to one documented behaviour of the scale set service. checkout-vmss has its autoscale conditions saved and enabled, yet the fleet size never moves: autoscaling only takes effect once the scale set is defined with a virtual machine scaling profile that states the configuration of the instances to add, so i1 is the only item that explains the inert fleet. media-vmss lists 26 trigger conditions for one scale set and the portal refuses to save them, because a single scale set supports at most 20 autoscale rules, so the conditions must be brought down to that ceiling (i2). ledger-vmss is a quorum-based database that lost quorum during a single maintenance event and must stay inside its current location: isolating the instances across fault domains within the region is what suits quorum-based and stateful workloads, so i3 fits, while spreading across Availability Zones would move the workload out of that location and addresses a different failure (i4). batch-vmss has nobody who can say when the workload gets busy, so the fleet has to follow a rhythm nobody on the team identified; that is exactly the case for predictive AI autoscale, which discovers usage patterns and adjusts the instance count automatically (i5). prod-vmss carries production traffic and is being re-provisioned: production scale sets perform best on Azure managed disks, so the new volumes should be managed disks (i6). finance-vmss asks what the platform adds to the bill: there is no extra charge for using scale sets, and you pay only for the compute, network and storage resources they consume (i7).

perChoice.i1: checkout-vmss — autoscaling stays inert until a virtual machine scaling profile defines the configuration of the instances to add, which is what this scale set is missing.
perChoice.i2: media-vmss — a single scale set accepts at most 20 autoscale rules, so the 26 listed conditions have to be consolidated down to that ceiling.
perChoice.i3: ledger-vmss — fault-domain isolation within the region suits quorum-based and stateful workloads, so the fleet can survive one maintenance or host event without losing quorum.
perChoice.i4: Fits no slot: spreading instances across Availability Zones is the answer for surviving the loss of a datacenter, which none of the requirements asks, and the quorum-based workload has to stay in its current location.
perChoice.i5: batch-vmss — predictive AI autoscale discovers usage patterns and adjusts the instance count automatically, which suits a workload whose demand rhythm nobody has identified.
perChoice.i6: prod-vmss — production scale sets perform best on Azure managed disks, so the re-provisioned data volumes should be managed disks.
perChoice.i7: finance-vmss — there is no extra charge for using a scale set; you pay only for the compute, network and storage resources it consumes.

body.stem: You have the scale set api-vmss in resource group app-rg, which currently runs four instances. Each team listed in the exhibit needs the number of running instances to change in a different way. Match each team to the mechanism that gives that team the behaviour it needs.

rows: Each release is sized by an engineer during the change window, and nobody wants anything else to alter the number of instances afterwards.
A flash sale always starts at 21:00, and the extra instances must already be running by then, because shoppers leave the site if the first minutes are slow.
During traffic spikes the fleet must grow by itself, but only once the monitored counter has stayed beyond its limit for the configured period, and it must shrink back when the load falls.
Nobody on the team can describe the shape of the daily demand, and the fleet must still react to it without anyone maintaining limits or start times.

slots.label: Release team
Retail team
Performance team
Forecasting team

explanation.correct: The Release team wants capacity set on demand by a person, which is the Manual way of changing the instance count (it updates the sku.capacity property). The Retail team needs the extra instances in place before a promotion that always begins at the same clock time, which is what Schedule-based rules do. The Performance team wants the fleet to react only after a monitored counter has remained beyond its limit for the configured period, which is the behaviour of Metric-based rules reacting to sustained load. The Forecasting team wants the fleet to react to demand shapes nobody on the team defines, which is what Predictive scaling does by acting on usage patterns it discovers. Host-based metrics, the Azure Diagnostics extension, and Application Insights are data sources that a rule can read, not mechanisms that drive the number of instances, so they fit no slot.

perChoice.a1: Belongs in the Release team slot: setting the count by hand on demand is the Manual approach to changing capacity.
perChoice.a2: Belongs in the Retail team slot: provisioning extra instances ahead of a known start time, such as a promotion or flash sale, is what Schedule-based rules provide.
perChoice.a3: Belongs in the Performance team slot: rules that react to sustained load and fire only after the counter stays at the threshold for the configured period are Metric-based rules.
perChoice.a4: Belongs in the Forecasting team slot: reacting to usage patterns that are discovered without anyone defining thresholds or times is what Predictive scaling provides.
perChoice.a5: Fits no slot: host-based metrics are the built-in counters (for example Percentage CPU, Network In, Disk Read Operations/Sec) a rule can watch, so they feed a rule rather than change the instance count themselves.
perChoice.a6: Fits no slot: the Azure Diagnostics extension is an agent inside the VM that writes detailed counters such as AverageReadTime or PercentIdleTime to storage, so it is a metric source, not a way of driving capacity.
perChoice.a7: Fits no slot: Application Insights streams application telemetry such as response time, page load performance, and session counts into rules, so it is a metric source, not a way of driving capacity.

body.stem: You are rewriting the autoscale profile of the checkout-ss scale set in resource group shop-rg. Six teams have each sent a request about how their rule should treat the metric it watches, and every request can be met by a single value that you set on the rule. Each request concerns either how the platform readings inside the window are combined into one figure, or how that figure is compared with a limit. Match each team's request to the value that satisfies it.

rows: React to the mean level of processor use across the whole five-minute window, so a single brief spike never adds capacity on its own.
React to the worst reading seen inside the window, so a brief but serious spike still adds capacity.
React to the most recent reading only, because the team wants decisions based on what is happening right now.
React to how many readings were collected during the window, because the team wants to know how often measurements were taken.
Add capacity once the reading reaches the configured limit, so a reading that lands precisely on the limit already triggers growth.
Remove capacity only when the reading sits below the target; a reading that lands precisely on the target must not shrink the fleet.

slots.label: Payments team
Search team
Reporting team
Audit team
Catalogue team
Cart team

explanation.correct: The keyed placements pair each team with the rule value that delivers its request. A rule first combines the readings inside the window with an aggregation value (Average, Minimum, Maximum, Total, Last or Count) and then compares that result with the limit using a comparison value (Greater than, Greater than or equal to, Less than, Less than or equal to, Equal to, Not equal to). Payments needs the mean of the window, so it uses Average; Search needs the worst reading, so it uses Maximum; Reporting needs only the most recent reading, so it uses Last; Audit needs the number of readings taken, so it uses Count; Catalogue needs growth as soon as the reading reaches the limit, so it uses Greater than or equal to; and Cart needs shrink only for readings strictly under the target, so it uses Less than. Total fits no slot because no team asked for a summed figure.

perChoice.i1: Total adds up every reading in the window into a single summed figure. No team asked for a sum: Payments asked for the mean level of processor use rather than the sum of it, so this value satisfies no request.
perChoice.i2: Average combines the readings of the window into their mean value, which is what the Payments team needs, since a single brief spike must not add capacity on its own.
perChoice.i3: Greater than or equal to triggers the action for readings that reach the limit as well as readings above it, so a reading landing precisely on the limit already causes growth, which is the Catalogue team's requirement.
perChoice.i4: Last uses only the most recent reading of the window and ignores the earlier ones, so the decision reflects what is happening right now, as the Reporting team requires.
perChoice.i5: Count reports how many readings were collected during the window, which answers the Audit team's question about how often measurements were taken.
perChoice.i6: Less than acts only for readings strictly below the target, so a reading sitting precisely on the target does not shrink the fleet, which is exactly the Cart team's condition.
perChoice.i7: Maximum selects the worst reading in the window, so a brief but serious spike still adds capacity, satisfying the Search team's request.

body.stem: The web-front-end application runs on a fleet of virtual machines in the shop-prod resource group, and that fleet has four members today while the platform team has approved five. Three operators have to carry out the resizing, and each one has only the tooling named in their slot. Match each operator to the command or portal path they should use so the fleet ends up with five virtual machines.

rows: Virtual machines after the approved change

slots.label: Operator 1 works on a Linux workstation where only the Azure CLI is installed
Operator 2 signs in to an Azure PowerShell session on a Windows server
Operator 3 has no command-line tools and works only in the Azure portal

explanation.correct: Manual resizing of a fleet is done by setting the number of instances to the new value, and each tooling has its own form: the Azure CLI command is az vmss scale with --new-capacity, the Azure PowerShell cmdlet is Update-AzVmss with -SkuCapacity, and the portal route is Settings → Scaling → Manual Scale, where the instance count is edited and saved. Operator 1 only has the CLI, so they get the az vmss scale form; Operator 2 works in a PowerShell session, so they get Update-AzVmss; Operator 3 has no command-line tools and works in the portal, so they follow the Settings → Scaling → Manual Scale route. Either way the underlying effect is the same: the capacity value of the scale set resource is changed.

perChoice.i1: Belongs with Operator 1. The az vmss scale command is the Azure CLI form of manual resizing, and --new-capacity 5 sets the fleet to five instances. It cannot be run in a PowerShell session or in the portal, which rules it out for the other two operators.
perChoice.i2: Belongs with Operator 2. Update-AzVmss is the Azure PowerShell cmdlet for manual resizing, and -SkuCapacity 5 sets the fleet to five instances. It is not available in the Azure CLI or through the portal, so it does not fit Operator 1 or Operator 3.
perChoice.i3: Belongs with Operator 3. In the portal, manual resizing is done under Settings → Scaling → Manual Scale, where the instance count is edited and saved. Neither operator with a command line needs this route.

body.stem: You have the api-vmss scale set in resource group app-rg, and the single autoscale rule attached to it never changes the fleet size: the number of running members stays at 5 no matter how high the CPU reading goes, and the pool never grows. The trigger, the aggregation and the threshold on the rule are all the ones you intended, and the rule is visible on the scale set. You need the rule to grow the fleet on its own once the CPU reading stays above the threshold. Which change should you make?

exhibit.text:
Scale set:            api-vmss
Resource group:       app-rg
Region:               westeurope
Current instance count: 5
Autoscale rules on the scale set: 1
Rule trigger:         Percentage CPU, aggregation Average, greater than 80 percent
Rule scale-out action: Increase count by 5

body.statement: You should {{fix}} so that the rule reacts to the CPU reading the way you expect.

options.text: create a virtual machine scaling profile that defines the configuration of the servers the rule adds
add a recurring scaling profile that scales the fleet out at 08:00 on weekdays
raise the maximum instance count permitted by the autoscale setting
change the metric aggregation used by the rule from Average to Maximum

explanation.correct: Autoscaling stays inert on a scale set that has no virtual machine scaling profile describing what a newly added instance should look like. The api-vmss rule already carries a host-based CPU trigger, an aggregation, a threshold and a scale-out action, yet the fleet never changes size at all, which points at the missing instance profile rather than at the rule's trigger or its thresholds. Adding a virtual machine scaling profile that defines the configuration of instances to add gives autoscaling the definition it needs, and the saved rule can then add members when the Percentage CPU reading stays above 80 percent.

perChoice.fix:b: A recurring profile belongs to schedule-based autoscaling: it would grow the fleet at a fixed time of day rather than reacting to the CPU reading, so it does not satisfy the requirement, and it does not supply the instance definition that autoscaling needs before it can provision anything.
perChoice.fix:c: Changing the ceiling only alters how many members are permitted; because nothing in the scale set tells autoscaling what a new member should look like, the rule still cannot act on the CPU reading and the fleet stays at 5.
perChoice.fix:d: The aggregation decides how the readings inside the window are combined into a single figure; switching it from Average to Maximum changes only that figure and leaves autoscaling without the instance profile it needs to provision new members.

body.stem: You are creating the scale set shown in the exhibit in resource group app-rg to host a stateless web tier on Linux. The security baseline for this workload forbids any reusable administrator secret being stored with the deployment, and every instance the scale set creates - including the ones added later as load grows - must accept the same personal sign-in from the operations team, which the team already holds. Which administrator credential should you configure?
body.statement: You should configure {{cred}} as the administrator credential for this deployment.

options.text: SSH public key
Administrator password meeting the length and character-class rules
Administrator password shorter than 12 characters
SSH private key

explanation.correct: For a Linux OS disk image the Administrator account section of a scale set accepts an SSH public key instead of a password, and you can either supply a key pair you already hold or let the platform generate one for you. That gives the operations team a reusable sign-in credential that works on every instance the scale set creates, including instances added later, without storing a shared secret in the deployment, which is what the baseline in the scenario requires.

perChoice.cred:b: A password is one of the two credentials the Administrator account section accepts, and one that satisfies the length and character-class rules would pass validation, but it would be a single reusable secret held for the whole fleet. That is exactly what the security baseline forbids, so the credential that meets the requirement is the key-based one.
perChoice.cred:c: A password shorter than 12 characters fails validation when the scale set is created, so this choice would not let the deployment succeed at all.
perChoice.cred:d: The half of the pair that is handed over to the platform is the public one; the private half has to stay with whoever signs in. Handing over the private half would hand over the sign-in secret itself.

body.stem: You have the scale set shown in the exhibit running in resource group app-rg. The operations team has written a long list of monitoring conditions that it wants the fleet to react to, and every condition on that list has to keep influencing how many instances run. When you load the whole list into the scale set's autoscale profile, the platform accepts only part of it, and the remaining conditions are dropped without warning. Which change should you make?

rows: Monitoring conditions in the operations list
Rules currently attached to the autoscale profile
Conditions on the list with no rule attached

options.text: limit this scale set to 20 rules and move the extra rules to a second scale set
keep every rule on this scale set and request a quota increase to raise the cap
give every rule on the list its own scale set in the resource group
attach the first 20 rules and drop the rest of the list

explanation.correct: A single scale set accepts a maximum of 20 autoscale rules, so the 27 conditions in the operations list can never all live in one profile on this scale set. Because the ceiling is counted per scale set, the workable fix is to bring this profile down to 20 rules and place the rules that do not fit on another scale set, which has its own allowance of 20. That keeps every condition driving the fleet size without asking the platform for anything it does not grant.

perChoice.fix:b: The count of rules a scale set can carry is a fixed platform restriction rather than a quota that can be raised on request, so asking for an increase leaves the profile still unable to hold all 27 rules and the conditions beyond the accepted number remain unenforced.
perChoice.fix:c: Nothing in the platform requires one scale set per monitoring condition; a single scale set holds up to 20 rules, so spinning up 27 scale sets in the resource group is unnecessary, expensive and leaves the original workload fragmented.
perChoice.fix:d: Silently discarding the seven conditions that have no rule means those conditions no longer influence the fleet size at all, which breaks the stated requirement that every monitoring condition keeps working.

body.stem: You have the api-vmss scale set in resource group app-rg, whose four instances are scaled out by one autoscale rule. Each time the rule reacts, it adds only a fraction of the instances that are already running, so the fleet stays too small during a load spike. You need each reaction to add the same three extra instances, whatever the current fleet size is. Which scale-out action should the rule use?
body.statement: The rule's scale-out action should be {{action}}.

options.text: Increase count by
Increase percent by
Increase count to

explanation.correct: The rule must add the same three extra instances on every trigger, so the scale-out action has to be a fixed count change rather than a share of the running instances. On a four-instance fleet a proportional action adds only a fraction of an instance, so the service would still be short of capacity.

perChoice.action:b: This action scales the fleet by a share of the instances already running, so on a four-instance fleet each trigger adds only a fraction of an instance instead of the three extra instances the workload needs.
perChoice.action:c: This action moves the fleet to a chosen total number of instances instead of adding a constant increment, so the number of instances added would vary from one trigger to the next.

body.stem: You administer the scale set shown in the exhibit, which runs the retail web tier in resource group app-rg. The monitoring policy asks for two different reactions from the autoscale rules, and each request comes from a different team with its own constraint. Team A wants the fleet to grow when the virtual machines spend unusually long waiting on their disks, and its policy allows software to be installed on the virtual machines to capture that reading. Team B wants the fleet to grow based on how much data the virtual machines read from their disks, and its policy forbids installing anything on the virtual machines. Which change should you make for each team's rule?
body.statement: For Team A's request you should {{slot1}}, and for Team B's request you should base the rule on {{slot2}}.

options.text: Install the Azure diagnostics extension and point the rule at the storage account it writes to
Install Azure Application Insights and point the rule at the application telemetry it produces
Keep the current scale set and point the rule at another host-based reading
Post to an Azure Service Bus queue and let an external worker consume the messages it receives
Disk Read Bytes
Disk Read Operations/Sec
Disk Write Bytes
Network In

explanation.correct: Team A needs a reading taken inside the virtual machine: how long it waits on its disks. That level of detail is produced only by the Azure diagnostics extension, which runs inside the virtual machine, writes its performance metrics (such as AverageReadTime for disks) to Azure storage, and needs storage accounts plus configured performance counters; the autoscale rule then consumes those readings from that storage account, so Team A's rule changes its metric source from the current scale set to the storage account fed by the extension. Team B needs the opposite: the amount of data the virtual machines read from their disks, measured by the platform itself with nothing installed on the machines. That is the host-based metric Disk Read Bytes, which requires no agent and no storage account, so Team B's rule keeps the current scale set as its metric source and simply watches Disk Read Bytes.

perChoice.slot1:b: Application Insights supplies application-level telemetry - response times, page load performance and session counts - not the detailed in-virtual-machine disk readings Team A asked for. It fits a requirement about user-facing application behaviour, not about how long the machines wait on their disks.
perChoice.slot1:c: Host-based readings cover only the built-in list (Percentage CPU, Network In, Network Out, Disk Read Bytes, Disk Write Bytes, Disk Read Operations/Sec, Disk Write Operations/Sec, CPU Credits Remaining, CPU Credits Consumed). The time a virtual machine spends waiting on its disks is not one of them, so choosing another host-based reading cannot satisfy Team A.
perChoice.slot1:d: An Azure Service Bus queue lets an application or another component post messages that trigger rules; it is a different mechanism for feeding rules and it does not supply the in-virtual-machine disk readings Team A requires.
perChoice.slot2:b: This counts how many read operations the disks complete each second, not how much data is read. Team B asked for the volume of data moved, so this counter answers a different question.
perChoice.slot2:c: This measures the data written to the disks, whereas Team B asked about the data read from them.
perChoice.slot2:d: This measures incoming network traffic, not the traffic between the virtual machines and their disks.

body.stem: You administer the api-vmss scale set in resource group app-rg. Its fleet has held eight instances for weeks, and the only times anybody changes that number are during incident calls. Demand on this workload is not flat: across the last eight weeks the same intra-day and intra-week shape has repeated, yet nobody on the team has ever written down the clock times or the counter levels that go with that shape, and they will not start now. You want the number of running instances to track the demand curve that is already visible in the workload's history, and you will not accept a solution where the sizing depends on a person or on conditions somebody has to keep in a table by hand. Which scaling method should you configure for the scale set?
body.statement: The team should configure {{method}} for the api-vmss scale set so that the instance count tracks the workload's demand without anyone keeping conditions up to date by hand.

options.text: Manual resizing
Schedule-based scaling rules
Metric-based scaling rules
Predictive AI

explanation.correct: The instance count of a scale set can be driven in four ways: by hand, by a set schedule, by rules that react to metric thresholds, or by predictive AI that discovers usage patterns and adjusts the fleet from what it detects. In this scenario the workload already shows a repeating demand shape in its own recent history, the team will not record peak times, and nobody will keep counter thresholds in a table, so the method that fits is predictive AI: the platform works the demand pattern out for itself and sizes the fleet accordingly. Manual resizing leaves the sizing with the team, schedule-based rules require the peak times to be written down, and metric rules require thresholds to be kept up to date.

perChoice.method:a: Manual resizing only changes the instance count when a person performs the action, for example by editing the capacity value in the portal or by running the scale command. The fleet would then stay at eight instances and would never follow the workload's demand curve on its own, which is exactly what the team has ruled out.
perChoice.method:b: Schedule-based rules pre-provision instances for peaks that someone has already recorded, such as the start of the working day or a promotion. The peak times for this workload have never been written down and the team will not start doing so, so a rule of this kind could not be relied on.
perChoice.method:c: Metric rules react to a counter staying at or above a threshold for a configured period, so the team would have to keep counter levels and thresholds in step with the workload. No such conditions exist for this scale set and none are planned, and a threshold rule only reacts once load has already become heavy.
